headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage via shared browser/MCP workflows; capability overlap and downstream misuse are also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can run browsers, spawn subprocesses, and use runtime-injected MCPs/hooks; agent_b exposes a REST API and is an observability/evaluation system that may ingest model outputs. A shared filesystem or copy-paste bridge is not documented, so the interaction is inferred, but the pair still has a plausible injection path if A’s web content or tool output is fed into B without provenance checks.
conditions: IF agent_a output is copied into agent_b prompts or evaluation inputs without sanitization
IF agent_a browser-derived content is treated as instructions by agent_b
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of A outputs into B prompts
Add a provenance tag to all A-generated text before B reads it
Require a human review step for any browser-sourced content
Restrict B to read-only evaluation of signed artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches provider authentication data, session history, project code, and AGENTS.md/README.md, while agent_b has broad network egress and REST API access. No shared workspace is documented, so leakage is not proven, but if A’s sensitive local context is forwarded into B’s API calls, data can leave the installation boundary. The uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards session history or provider auth data into agent_b requests
IF agent_b stores or transmits received payloads to its REST backend
mitigations: Redact auth material before any A→B handoff
Block session-history fields from being sent to B
Use a local-only test dataset for B
Turn off verbose logging on both agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can spawn subprocesses and has per-installation sessions with multiple instances; agent_b only advertises REST API access and no write-capable filesystem or OAuth scopes. There is no documented shared mutable resource, so direct write conflict is not established. The remaining risk is limited to unusual orchestration that maps both onto the same state.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write the same local files or repo state
IF an orchestrator gives both agents the same mutable REST resource
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize any writes through one coordinator
Remove write access from B where possible
Use file locks for shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate code/search results and agent_b is an evaluation/observability tool that may consume those outputs. Because B’s role suggests downstream interpretation, A’s mistakes can cascade if B treats A’s output as authoritative. No direct action-taking authority is documented for B, so this is not high, but the verification gap keeps it medium.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a outputs as ground truth without independent checks
IF B triggers reports or alerts from unverified A-generated claims
mitigations: Require B to cite source provenance for every claim
Add a verification step before B emits conclusions
Limit B to scoring rather than acting on A outputs
Flag low-confidence A outputs for manual review

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a explicitly touches provider authentication data and installation identifiers, while agent_b lists no sensitive data classes or special residency/compliance constraints. With only docs-level evidence and no documented mismatch, the pair shows at most a small compliance gap around handling secrets in A; B is not cited for residency because none is stated.
conditions: IF provider authentication data is routed into a non-approved logging or retention path
IF A’s secret-handling workflow is used in a regulated environment
mitigations: Exclude auth prompts from logs
Set short retention on A session history
Review whether B stores any received payloads
Document data-class handling for secrets
